learn.title: A loop in one line
learn.body: A `for` loop puts the start, the test and the change on a single line, separated by semicolons. It is the natural choice when you know how many times to repeat.

learn.title: Count from zero
learn.body: Start `i` at 0, repeat while `i < 3`, add 1 each time.

learn.title: The three parts
learn.body: Inside the parentheses: first an initialisation, `int i = 0`, which runs once. Second a condition, `i < 3`, tested before each pass. Third an update, `i++`, run after each pass. It is the same pattern as a while loop.

learn.title: Counting from zero
learn.body: Programmers usually count from 0 and stop with `i < n`. This repeats exactly n times: with n equal to 3 it gives 0, 1, 2. Writing `i <= n` instead runs one extra time. That mistake is called an off-by-one error.

learn.title: Adding 1 to 10
learn.body: Here we want 1 to 10 both included, so we use `<=`.

learn.title: Other steps
learn.body: The update can be anything. `i += 2` counts by twos, and `i--` counts down by one. In the loop `for (int i = 10; i > 0; i -= 3)` the values are 10, 7, 4 and 1.

learn.title: Tracing the sum
learn.body: Follow the first passes of `sum += i`.
A variable declared in the `for` parentheses exists only inside that loop.

questions.prompt: How many times does `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)` run its block?
How many times does `for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++)` run?
questions.explanation: `i` takes the values 1 to 5, five values.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of 1 to 10 computed by the loop? Type the number.
The three parts of a for loop are separated by \_\_.
What is the last number printed by `for (int i = 10; i > 0; i -= 3)`? Type it.
questions.explanation: The values are 10, 7, 4 and 1. After 1 comes -2, which fails `i > 0`.

choices: A loop that runs one time too many or too few
questions.explanation: It usually comes from choosing `<` or `<=` wrongly.
Start at 1 and keep going while `i <= 3`.

questions.explanation: These three parts replace the three parts of a while loop.
